How does one define the type of C^k[0,1] of functions from [0, 1] to ℝ, differentiable k times, the kth derivative is continuous?

In particular, on (0,1) the derivative would be the two-sided derivative, but at 0 and 1 the derivative would be a one-sided derivative. The derivative should be a function from C^k[0,1] → C^{k-1}[0,1], and if there the ℝ-vector space instance on C^k[0,1], and the ring instance on C^k[0,1] already exist that would be great to know too!

I thought ContDiff would try to be this, but it requires the domain type to be a commgroup.

import Mathlib

variable (f : unitInterval → ℝ) in
#check Continuous f -- works

variable (f : unitInterval → ℝ) in
#check ContDiff ℝ 0 f -- fails

variable (f : unitInterval → ℝ) in
#check ContDiff ℝ 1 f -- fails

(for another reference on the type I'm looking at, there is this note which defines C^1[-1, 1])

docs#ContDiff is for functions between normed spaces, that's why it requires the domain to be among other things an additive commutative group. To talk about functions from the unit interval you can use docs#ContMDiff from the API on manifolds instead:

import Mathlib

open scoped Manifold ContDiff

variable {k : ℕ∞ω}

#check ContMDiffMap (𝓡∂ 1) 𝓘(ℝ, ℝ) unitInterval ℝ k
it carries a module and ring structure already too through docs#ContMDiffMap.module and docs#ContMDiffMap.ring
Can's you just use ContDiffOn? ContDiffWithinAt makes sure that the derivatives considered on the boundary points are one-sided derivatives.

There's an "XY" problem here: are you sure you want functions on the unit interval? In Lean (and other type-theory-based proof assistants) one has to distinguish between "working with functions on [0, 1]" and "working with functions on ℝ and ignoring their values outside [0, 1]" – and, counterintuitively, the latter is almost always easier to do. (A common affliction for novice Lean users is "subtype-itis" – the mistaken belief that every subset/subring/whatever you encounter has to be made into a subtype – with experience you learn to avoid subtypes in almost all cases.)

If you really want the subtype, then ContMDiff is the way to go; but if you can avoid it and work with functions on ℝ then go for ContDiffOn.

Thanks everyone! ContMDiffMap looks great to take a look at!

I didn't realise that ContDiffWithinAt would give the one-sided derivative, I thought for the indicator function on [0, 1] defined from ℝ to ℝ it would hold for the set (0, 1) but not [0, 1]. I think that's my fault for reading the file docstring of ContDiff.Defs but not the docstring for ContDiffWithinAt :sweat_smile:

if you can avoid it and work with functions on ℝ then go for ContDiffOn.

Yes I did consider this! However I was thinking of "the functions are 0 outside of [0, 1]" instead of "the function's values outside of [0, 1] are ignored", because AIUI the later requires taking a quotient (I would want two functions which agreed on [0, 1] but with different values outside to be equal). (Not that there's anything wrong with taking a quotient, I was just not sure if it would cause other different problems down the line). ContDiffWithinAt seems like the right approach for "the functions are 0 outside of [0, 1]"
